opening.headline: We explain what terms like ASL mean, the structure of the Responsible Scaling Policy, and how to read a risk report.
body: If your security team sees something like “ASL-3 safeguards in place” in your model presentation and asks, “What is ASL and what does it have to do with our contracts?” how do you respond? If we don't know the terminology, we can't read the provider's safety commitments or incorporate them into our plans.

In this class, you will read the Risk Assessment and Mitigation and Frontier Safety Roadmap and Public Risk Report from RSP v3.4 as of 2026-10. Distinguish between the ASL/Proficiency Threshold descriptions in previous editions and the promises of the current document, and determine how providers' actual actions impact our usage plans.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the structure and risk report of Responsible Scaling Policy
Distinguish between previous versions of ASL descriptions and current risk assessment and mitigation commitments

screens.title: What does the word ASL mean?
screens.lead:
Follow the questions asked by a security officer who was reading the model presentation. It's good to read while thinking about what kind of judgment you might be stuck in when you don't know the terminology.

As of 2026-10, RSP v3.4 is a policy that reads together Risk Mitigation Measures, Frontier Safety Roadmap, and Risk Reports. Descriptions of past ASL stages do not determine all current training and deployment conditions.

paragraphs: The announcement of the new model says "ASL-3 safety measures applied." the security team asks. “What is ASL and what does it have to do with our contract?” There is no one on the team who can answer this question.

Without knowing what ASL is, we can't read the safety measures promised by our providers and determine how they impact our work. Conversely, if you know the structure, you can read from one line of the announcement how the provider evaluated the model's capabilities and what safety measures were added.
This class covers how to read Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy and how it is structured and through which documents it is disclosed.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Knowing the terminology and memorizing the content of the policy are different. This class focuses on reading structures that work even when policies change.

screens.outro: First, let me recall my experience encountering this document.

screens.title: Have you ever read RSP
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't enter or submit your answer, so think for yourself first and then click.

items.prompt: Have you ever read the Responsible Scaling Policy?
items.answer: Even if you've never read it, knowing this policy exists is the first step. RSP is a publicly available risk governance framework used by Anthropic to reduce the catastrophic risks that frontline AI systems can pose.

items.prompt: Did you know that policies are updated in multiple versions?
items.answer: RSP has been updated several times since it was first released in September 2023, and the page contains both current and previous versions. Therefore, understanding the structure and concepts is more useful than memorizing a specific version of a phrase.

items.prompt: Did you know that risk reports are released separately?
items.answer: System cards are released with each model release, and separately, risk reports are released on a regular basis. The two documents answer different questions and should be read together to provide a complete view of the provider's risk assessment.

screens.outro: Now that we've organized the background, let's start by checking the structure of RSP through the cards.

screens.title: Core concepts of RSP
screens.lead: The following cards explain five concepts needed to understand RSP: Selecting a card flips it over, and selecting the right arrow moves to the next card.

cards.back: This is the principle of designing a response based on the potential risk. Current policy requirements and future improvement goals are read separately.
This is the framework that explained safety and security levels in previous versions. The entire current policy should not be replaced by a historical step table.
Identify specifically which risks are lowered and under what conditions. The application target, conditions, and verification basis are more important than the name.
Read about our goals and progress toward improving risk mitigation. Distinguish between changes in objectives and policy obligations.
We look at the risks of models and activities, mitigation measures and the basis for judgment. Check the target model and base date first.

screens.outro: Now that we've confirmed the concepts, let's tab compare the order in which we read the current policy and the differences between past editions.

screens.title: Distinguish between current policy and past versions
screens.lead: Check the order in which you read the current policy and what to look out for when comparing past versions.

tabs.label: current version
tabs.body: As of 2026-10, the current document is RSP v3.4. It is read based on the structure after the complete overhaul of v3.0, and explanations from previous versions are separated by historical context.

tabs.label: Risks and Actions
tabs.body: Rather than memorizing the risk names, read the target capabilities, evaluation basis, application conditions and responses in a table.

tabs.label: Security and Distribution
tabs.body: Check security controls such as weight protection and distribution controls such as user access and monitoring.

tabs.label: Roadmap and Report
tabs.body: Read the improvement goals in the roadmap and the basis for evaluation and judgment in the risk report. Do not treat the two documents as promises of the same nature.

tabs.label: Compare past phrases
tabs.body: We do not cite past ASL clarifications or blanket discontinuation promises as current rules. When comparing, record the version and enforcement date of the document.

screens.outro: Now that we've identified the versions of the policy, let's read the risk report, which discloses the basis for the decision.

screens.title: Commentary: Read the risk report
screens.lead: Your instructor will walk you through the steps in which order to read the risk report. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: Identify the nature of the report
steps.body: Anthropic says it aims to issue risk reports every three to six months. While the system card that appears every time a model is released is a model-specific analysis, the risk report looks more broadly at not only the model's attributes but also risk mitigation measures such as security controls and deployment safeguards.

steps.title: Check range
steps.body: The report is not a performance table for one specific model, but rather a risk assessment of Anthropic's activities as a whole. We also cover internal models that are not yet released. So when reading, first check which models this report is targeting.

steps.title: Follow the risk categories
steps.body: The report addresses one by one the categories of catastrophic risks highlighted by the policy. These categories include misalignment in high-risk environments, automated research and development in critical areas, and chemical and biological weapons production. At the end, considerations across different categories are discussed separately.

steps.title: Descriptive framework for each category
steps.body: For each risk category, we describe the threat model, the corresponding AI model, current capabilities and behaviors, and risk mitigation measures. A threat model summarizes the pathways through which the model may contribute to a risk, as well as an idea of ​​their likelihood and magnitude. This framework also serves as a reference when our organization writes its own risk assessment.

steps.title: Classification of comprehensive evaluation
steps.body: The overall evaluation distinguishes between marginal risk compared to other developers and absolute risk relative to the industry as a whole. The same number has different meanings depending on what standard you use it for, so when reading, you need to check which side you are talking about.

screens.outro: Now that we know how to read the report, let's compare how increasing the safety level affects our ability to use our features.

screens.title: Commentary: Impact of increasing safety levels on feature delivery
screens.lead: Switch between the two views to compare how the provider's safety judgments inform your use of our features.

states.label: What happens on the provider side
states.body: As capabilities increase, so do safety requirements. The risk report describes a structure in which the strongest models will be offered to select customers first, and versions with additional safeguards will be provided separately for general access. In this structure, even models of the same series may have different approaches and additional controls. Policies are continuously updated, so you should check the current wording and terms of application along with the concepts.

states.label: What changes in our usage plan
states.body: Enhanced safeguards can touch the user experience in the form of monitoring and access control. Some features may be limited in the standard access version, and some requests may require additional verification. Therefore, it is safer to plan use by checking the current version of the policy and the actual application conditions, and to prepare alternative means if the core business depends on a specific function. Include checking the provider's announcement for ASL language and access conditions. Comparing the two views, it becomes clear that while changes on the provider side are out of our control, it is up to us to read and respond to those changes. If you get into the habit of reading changes in advance, you can move on to the alternatives you have prepared rather than being surprised when functionality is limited. Designate a person in charge to regularly check announcements and policy pages, and also determine the frequency at which the verification results will be reflected in usage plans.

screens.outro: I will summarize the contents so far into one paragraph.

screens.title: As capabilities increase, safety requirements also increase.
screens.lead: Let's tie the contents of this class into one principle. Read the paragraph below and move on to the final summary.

paragraphs: As of 2026-10, RSP v3.4 is a policy that reads together Risk Mitigation Measures, Frontier Safety Roadmap, and Risk Reports. Descriptions of past ASL stages do not determine all current training and deployment conditions.

Risk reports are documents that regularly disclose how these promises are being kept in practice. Contains threat models, current capabilities, mitigation actions, and comprehensive assessments by category. By reading each line of the announcement and each section of the report together, you can follow the basis for the provider's judgment.

From a usage planning perspective, keep two things in mind: Policies need to be based on concepts as they are updated, and approaches and additional controls may change as safety levels increase, so alternative means should be in place for core functions.

Lastly, record the provider's commitments separately from your organization's controls. RSP is a promise that the provider will keep to its model, and our organization's policies and settings are promises that we must keep. If you tabulate the overlapping points and empty points, you can use them as a basis for both contract review and security review.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: Please record the version, enforcement date, scope of application, obligations and goals.

checks.intro: Check out the core concepts of RSP we just saw. Just match the term with an appropriate description. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Match the key concepts and explanations of RSP.
right: Explain the risks of the model/activity, mitigation measures, and basis for judgment
Responses applied to reduce a specific risk
Principles for designing response intensity according to risk
Documentation confirming safety improvement goals and progress
checks.correctFeedback: We have clearly distinguished the four concepts of RSP.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Try to separate principles, responses, goals, and basis for judgment and reconnect them.
checks.explain: Proportional protection is the principle, mitigation measures are the response, the roadmap is the improvement goal, and the risk report is the basis for evaluation and judgment.

checks.intro: Apply what you see in the commentary to your usage plans. Just choose the most appropriate implications.
checks.q: The report states that the most powerful model will be offered to select customers first, followed by a general access version with additional safety features. What are the implications for usage plans?
options: The standard access version always has the same features and same controls.
Just memorize the current wording of the RSP document so you don't have to change your plan.
Even within the same family, approaches and additional controls may be different.
Increasing the safety level has no effect on the user experience.
checks.correctFeedback: I read your implication correctly that the approach and additional controls may vary.
checks.incorrectFeedback: This explanation misses the point that increasing safety levels can have implications for user experience.
checks.explain: As capabilities increase, safety requirements also increase, and safeguards such as monitoring and access control may become part of the user experience. Policy versions change, so planning is based on the concept of safety levels and thresholds.

wrong.0: Access and additional controls may vary depending on the version.
wrong.1: Policies are updated, so you should check the concepts and current applicable terms.
wrong.3: Upgraded safety features can reach the user experience.

glossary.def: This is an abbreviation for Responsible Scaling Policy, which is Anthropic's risk governance policy that requires safety measures in proportion to capabilities.
This is a term used to describe the safety and security level of past policies. Coverage of current measures should be checked with the current RSP.
That capability is a specific level of AI capability that will require stronger safeguards than the current baseline.
This is a regularly published report containing categories of threat models, their current capabilities, mitigation measures, and overall assessment.

misconceptions.myth: ASL is the rating of the product.
misconceptions.fact: ASL is a level of safety and security standards tailored to the model's capabilities. A higher level does not mean a better product, but more stringent measures are required.

misconceptions.myth: Once a policy is set, it is fixed.
misconceptions.fact: RSP has been updated several times since it was first released, and current and previous versions are released together. Rather than memorizing phrases, you should read based on structure and concept.

misconceptions.myth: A risk report is a performance table for one model.
misconceptions.fact: The risk report is a risk assessment of Anthropic's activities as a whole, rather than a specific model, and even covers models that have not yet been released. It should be read with a focus on the threat model, mitigation measures, and comprehensive assessment.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: As capabilities increase, so do safety requirements.
Distinguish between the current RSP's actions, roadmap and risk report.
Past ASL statements do not equate to current overall policy.
Risk reports regularly publish threat models, mitigation measures and comprehensive assessments.
closing.reflectionLead: The questions below are for your own reflection only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: When the safety level increases, what access conditions can be attached to the functions we use? Pick the one feature you rely on the most and think of alternatives.
